prayer.text: Saint Brigid of Kildare, pray for us.

cues.text: A Refusal That Shaped a Life
Born around 451 near Faughart in County Louth, Brigid grew into a young woman whose family, of evident standing, arranged several good marriage offers.
She consistently and firmly declined them, determined instead to consecrate her life entirely to God.

She received the religious veil from St. Macaille, and, together with seven companions, set out to build a life of prayer and service that would eventually reshape the religious landscape of southern Ireland.
The Church of the Oak
Settling at last on the plains of Magh Life, Brigid established her community beneath a great oak tree.
She gave her foundation the enduring name Cill Dara , "the church of the oak," from which modern Kildare takes its name.
Her monastery grew rapidly into something unusual even by the standards of the vigorous early Irish Church: a double monastery .
It housed a community of women under Brigid's own governance and a community of men, for whom she selected a bishop, St. Conleth, to share in the community's spiritual leadership.
The importance of Kildare gave its abbesses considerable prestige, although the extent and continuity of their authority over other Irish convents should not be overstated.
A Reputation for Boundless Charity
The stories that gathered around Brigid's memory in the generations after her death are strikingly consistent in their central theme: an almost limitless generosity.

This generosity toward the poor, the hungry, and the suffering was so vivid in the popular imagination that later hagiography credited her with an almost magical ability to multiply food, drink, and alms for those in need.
Whatever the precise historical kernel beneath these legends, they preserve a genuine and treasured memory of this woman.
Of noble birth and real ecclesiastical authority, she was remembered above all for her tender mercy toward those who had nothing.
That reputation survived fifteen centuries of retelling essentially unchanged.
A Center of Learning and Art
Under Brigid's guidance, Kildare developed into far more than a monastery.
It became one of the great centers of religion, learning, and artistic craft in early medieval Ireland.
Kildare was home to a renowned scriptorium whose illuminated Gospel book has since been lost.
Centuries later, the visiting chronicler Giraldus Cambrensis praised it as a work of nearly miraculous beauty.
It testified to the extraordinary flourishing of Christian art and scholarship that grew up under her foundation's protection.
Mary of the Gael
Across the centuries following her death, Brigid's stature in the memory of the Irish Church grew to a level matched by only two other figures.
These were St. Patrick , apostle of Ireland, and St. Columba , apostle to Scotland.
Together, they came to be regarded as among the principal patrons and foundational figures of Irish Christianity.
Devotion to Brigid earned her the enduring popular title "Mary of the Gael," a name reflecting genuine theological caution.
No one confused her with the Mother of God, yet the title also expressed the depth of affection an entire people came to feel for this one abbess of Kildare.
Legacy
Brigid died at Kildare on February 1, 525.
Her feast, still kept on that date across Ireland and the wider Irish diaspora, has long been associated with spring’s first stirrings.
This season of returning warmth and new growth is fittingly linked to a saint remembered above all for warmth of heart.
To this day, Irish families continue the traditional practice of weaving a simple cross from rushes on her feast day.
This small, humble craft, passed down through countless generations, keeps alive the memory of a woman whose extraordinary generosity has never been forgotten in the most ordinary household gestures.
Fifteen centuries later, she still teaches every believer that a life given freely away, rather than hoarded or protected, is the life that a whole people will remember longest.
